titleStmt.title: Electrophysiological evidence for size invariance in masked picture repetition priming
titleStmt.author: Marianna D Eddy
Phillip J Holcomb

publicationStmt.p: Tag layer of the DHSS Meta-Tagging Project. The article text is reproduced from the staged copy named in sourceDesc and is not altered; the tags are held separately in standOff so that overlapping and nested spans are preserved.

bibl.title: Electrophysiological evidence for size invariance in masked picture repetition priming

person.p: the tag layer; a sentence written by the tagger about the paper, always anchored to a quotation but not itself a quotation

span.label: existence
span.quote: This experiment found that both early (N190/P190 effects) and later effects (N400) were invariant to size, whereas only the N190/P190 effect was invariant to mirror reflection.

span.label: masked repetition priming of pictures
span.quote: This experiment examined invariance in object representations through measuring event-related potentials (ERPs) to pictures in a masked repetition priming paradigm.

span.label: electrophysiology
span.quote: The EEG (250 Hz sampling rate, bandpass 0.01 and 40 Hz) was recorded continuously (SA Instruments amplifier, San Diego, CA) and ERPs were averaged time-locked to the onset of targets.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Object recognition proceeds hierarchically: perceptual overlap between prime and target must first be established before a higher-level semantic representation can be activated, so blocking the early overlap blocks the later effect.
span.quote: Taken together, the results of this set of experiments suggests that object recognition, more specifically, activating an object representation, occurs in a hierarchical fashion where overlapping perceptual information between the prime and target is necessary, although not always sufficient, to activate a higher level semantic representation.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Insufficient pooling: many neurons coding low-level features may fire to both prime and target, yet not enough of their activity converges to drive the sparser, more complex intermediate representation.
span.quote: It is possible that a large number of neurons are active to encode perceptual features of the prime object that overlap with the target object, but there is not sufficient activation to pool together to activate an intermediate representation that relies on a more complex integration of these features.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Receptive-field displacement: mirror reflection moves the prime-activated features outside the receptive fields of the cells that the target activates, so no priming benefit accrues.
span.quote: If the mirror reflection is placing visual features activated by the prime outside the receptive field of a cell activated for the target, then no benefit in priming would be expected.

span.label: mechanisms
span.term: Compensation cost: reconciling a prime and target that differ in both size and left-right orientation demands extra processing effort, which shows up as a reduced (here absent) N190/P190 priming effect.
span.quote: If a compensation process must equate the prime and target as the same when they are different sizes and mirror reflected, an increase in processing effort (as indicated by greater amplitude for the repeated condition and less of an N190/P190) would be expected, like the effect observed in the current experiment.

span.label: Object symmetry was not controlled, so the surviving early mirror effect may be an artefact of symmetric items.
span.quote: One factor that was not controlled for was how symmetrical objects were when mirror reflected.

span.label: The early mirror-reflection priming effect may reflect global shape overlap rather than internal object features.
span.quote: It is possible this effect was mainly driven by overlap in overall shape of the prime and target, rather than internal features.

span.label: No N300 effect was obtained in any condition, possibly because the rapid presentation rate merged it with the N400.
span.quote: One possibility for this could be the rapid presentation rate of the objects, leading to a streamlined process where the N300 effect is somehow combined or smeared with the N400.

span.label: twelve counterbalanced lists, so each repeated and unrepeated object appears an equal number of times across participants while appearing in only one condition for any single participant
span.note: eliminates: item effects - that a difference between repeated and unrepeated objects is a property of which objects happened to fall in which condition
span.quote: Twelve counterbalanced lists resulted in each repeated and unrepeated object being presented an equal number of times across participants, but each object being presented in only one trial for each participant.

span.label: invariance
span.quote: This experiment examined invariance in object representations through measuring event-related potentials (ERPs) to pictures in a masked repetition priming paradigm

span.label: masked repetition priming
span.quote: Previous masked repetition priming studies have found a cascade of priming effect sensitive to perceptual (N190/P190) and semantic (N400) properties of the stimulus

span.label: N190/P190
span.quote: The N190/P190 component is thought to reflect early perceptual processing of objects

span.label: N400
span.quote: The N400 is thought to reflect a general semantic mediated process or a process that activates a higher level representation of the object or word

span.label: mirror reflection
span.quote: The rearrangement of spatial configuration of parts (by mirror reflection) appears to be enough to attenuate the N400 effect, which suggests the hierarchical processing of perceptual features to semantic features was interrupted by this manipulation

span.label: object recognition
span.quote: Taken together, the results of this set of experiments suggests that object recognition, more specifically, activating an object representation, occurs in a hierarchical fashion where overlapping perceptual information between the prime and target is necessary, although not always sufficient, to activate a higher level semantic representation

span.label: PRIMING IS THE INSTRUMENT AND INVARIANCE IS THE SUBJECT, stated in the abstract's first sentence: `This experiment examined INVARIANCE IN OBJECT REPRESENTATIONS through measuring event-related potentials (ERPs) to pictures in a masked repetition priming paradigm.` Whether priming SURVIVES a transformation is the measurement of whether the representation is invariant to it - so the experiment is about object representation, and priming is the apparatus. The pickering2008 distinction (Q-744) in a third literature, after Argiris2021
span.quote: This experiment examined invariance in object representations through measuring event-related potentials (ERPs) to pictures in a masked repetition priming paradigm

span.label: NECESSARY, ALTHOUGH NOT ALWAYS SUFFICIENT - an explicit logical qualifier, which is rare enough in this corpus to be worth a row of its own. `Overlapping perceptual information between the prime and target is NECESSARY, ALTHOUGH NOT ALWAYS SUFFICIENT, to activate a higher level semantic representation.` Necessity and the denial of sufficiency in one clause, and the design earns both halves separately: the mirror condition gives early overlap WITHOUT the later effect (not sufficient), and the size-mirror condition removes the early effect and the later one with it (necessary). The record's mechanisms[0] paraphrases only the necessity half
span.quote: Taken together, the results of this set of experiments suggests that object recognition, more specifically, activating an object representation, occurs in a hierarchical fashion where overlapping perceptual information between the prime and target is necessary, although not always sufficient, to activate a higher level semantic representation

span.label: THE LATE STAGE IS MORE INVARIANT THAN THE EARLY ONE, which is the opposite of the obvious ordering. `The N400 unlike the N190/P190 appears to be FULLY invariant to size, since the repetition effect for the small prime condition DID NOT DIFFER from the repetition effect for the identity priming condition` - a null stated with its statistical basis attached. The early perceptual effect survives the same manipulation but pays for it: it `compensates for differences in size, BUT NOT WITHOUT A SMALL PROCESSING COST`. So invariance is not a property a representation has or lacks; it is graded, and it is cheaper further up
span.quote: Importantly though, the N400 unlike the N190/P190 appears to be fully invariant to size, since the repetition effect for the small prime condition did not differ from the repetition effect for the identity priming condition

span.label: THE ERP CASCADE TURNS `IS IT INVARIANT?` INTO `WHEN DOES IT STOP BEING INVARIANT?` The conclusion says exactly this: the results `help elucidate the TIME COURSE of previous fMRI findings of size invariance in adaptation paradigms and also WHEN during object processing left-right arrangement of objects becomes important for activating an object representation.` fMRI adaptation can say a region is invariant; a component sequence can say at which stage the invariance ends. That is the methodological reason this paper exists, and it is a claim about what its instrument can resolve rather than about objects
span.quote: The results of this study help elucidate the time course of previous fMRI findings of size invariance in adaptation paradigms and also when during object processing left-right arrangement of objects becomes important for activating an object representation

span.label: contradicts → Fiser and Biederman (2001)
span.quote: This finding of an attenuated N400 effect for the mirror reflected condition is inconsistent with the findings of Fiser and Biederman (2001) who found intact priming effects regardless of left-right orientation.

span.label: extends → Chauncey et al. (2008) masked size-priming study with words
span.quote: This finding is consistent with the findings of intact series of priming effects with changes in word size by Chauncey et al. (2008) as well as findings in neurophysiological studies (e.g., Ito et al., 1995 ) where a significant change in size still led to invariant firing the inferior temporal (IT) cortex of monkey.

span.label: builds-on → Eddy et al. (2006) masked repetition priming of pictures
span.quote: The aim of this experiment was to address how the series of ERP components observed in masked repetition picture priming ( Eddy et al., 2006 ) are affected by changes in physical features of the stimuli.

span.label: invariance —operationalised-as→ masked repetition priming
span.note: strength of the relation: 0.95 — The instrument relation, and the paper's own first sentence states it: invariance is examined THROUGH a masked repetition priming paradigm. Weighted 0.95 because this is a statement of what the experiment does, not an inference from its results.
span.quote: This experiment examined invariance in object representations through measuring event-related potentials (ERPs) to pictures in a masked repetition priming paradigm

span.label: N190/P190 —contrasted-with→ N400
span.note: differs in: WHICH TRANSFORMATION EACH TOLERATES. Both survive a halving of the prime; only the early one survives mirror reflection of the target. The two manipulations are therefore indistinguishable at the perceptual stage and separate at the semantic one, which is how the paper locates where left-right arrangement starts to matter · strength of the relation: 0.9 — THE PAPER'S CORE DISSOCIATION, and the span carries both arms of it so a reader cannot take half. Grounded on the abstract's result sentence rather than the discussion because this is the one place both components and both transformations appear together.
span.quote: This experiment found that both early (N190/P190 effects) and later effects (N400) were invariant to size, whereas only the N190/P190 effect was invariant to mirror reflection

span.label: mirror reflection —causes→ N400
span.note: direction on the measure: reduces · strength of the relation: 0.85 — `reduces` AND NOT `eliminates`, WHICH IS A Q-764 CALL AND IT WENT AGAINST THE OBVIOUS READING. The result sentence says `no significant N400 effect was observed` and the record's existing content_tags.findings[6] says the effect was `eliminated ... altogether` - but the discussion's own verb for the same result is ATTENUATE, and a non-significant effect is not a demonstrated zero. The paper's weaker word is the one inside the quote. Weight 0.85 and `appears to be` left in for the same reason.
span.quote: The rearrangement of spatial configuration of parts (by mirror reflection) appears to be enough to attenuate the N400 effect, which suggests the hierarchical processing of perceptual features to semantic features was interrupted by this manipulation

span.label: repeated-measures ANOVA
span.quote: For each time window we used repeated measures Analysis of Variance (ANOVA) to examine the differences in processing between each manipulation (identity, size, mirror manipulations).

span.label: Greenhouse-Geisser correction
span.quote: The Geisser and Greenhouse (1959) correction was applied to all repeated measures with more than one degree of freedom (df) (all p values reported for comparisons with more than 1 df are Greenhouse-Geisser corrected) and partial eta squared (η p 2 ) values were reported to assess effect size.

span.label: effect size (partial eta squared)
span.quote: The Geisser and Greenhouse (1959) correction was applied to all repeated measures with more than one degree of freedom (df) (all p values reported for comparisons with more than 1 df are Greenhouse-Geisser corrected) and partial eta squared (η p 2 ) values were reported to assess effect size.

span.label: t-test
span.quote: When a food prime was a normal size the d’ was 1.81 and when it was a small food prime the d’ was 1.71, suggesting that participants were NOT able to identify food objects in the prime position regardless of prime size (t(23) = 1.119, p = 0.275).

span.label: d-prime (signal detection sensitivity)
span.quote: The average d’ was calculated for probe food items in the prime position for identity food and small food primes (the primes for the other conditions involved the same manipulations).

span.label: mean
span.quote: Mean amplitude measurements were made in three time windows (early N190/P190 region 100–250 ms; N300 region 250–350 ms, and N400 region 350–500 ms).

span.label: standard deviation
span.quote: Twenty-four volunteers (13 female, M = 19.6 years old, SD = 1.2 years), undergraduate students at Tufts University, were paid $20 to participate in this experiment.

span.label: Masked repetition priming of pictures produced ERP effects that survived a halving of prime size at both the early (N190/P190) and late (N400) stages, but survived mirror reflection of the target only at the early stage.
span.quote: This experiment found that both early (N190/P190 effects) and later effects (N400) were invariant to size, whereas only the N190/P190 effect was invariant to mirror reflection.

span.label: Combining the two transformations, a small prime followed by a mirror-reflected target, abolished priming entirely, in every time window.
span.quote: The combination of a small prime and a mirror reflected target led to no significant priming effects.

span.label: Even in the earliest window, the small-prime-plus-mirror condition produced no reliable repetition effect (F<3, p>0.065).
span.quote: While significant repetition effects are observed for the small prime-identity target condition (see results above), when investigating repetition effects for the small prime – mirror reversal condition alone, no repetition effects are observed (F<3, p > 0.065) within this early time window (see Figure 6 and 7D ).

span.label: No significant N300 repetition effect appeared in any condition, which the authors attribute to the rapid presentation rate smearing the N300 into the N400.
span.quote: In terms of higher level processing, no significant N300 effects were observed for any of the conditions.

span.label: The N400 was fully size-invariant: the small-prime repetition effect was statistically indistinguishable from the identity repetition effect.
span.quote: Importantly though, the N400 unlike the N190/P190 appears to be fully invariant to size, since the repetition effect for the small prime condition did not differ from the repetition effect for the identity priming condition.

span.label: The early N190/P190 was only partially size-invariant: the effect was reliably present but smaller with a small prime, implying a processing cost for compensating the size difference.
span.quote: Therefore, this early effect is indexing processing of object features and shape in a way that compensates for differences in size, but not without a small processing cost associated with this compensation.

span.label: Mirror-reflecting the target eliminated the N400 repetition effect altogether.
span.quote: In our experiment when objects were mirror reflected, no significant N400 effect was observed.

span.label: The failure of priming in the combined small-prime/mirror-target condition is attributable to the mirror reflection rather than to the prime size, since small primes alone still primed and mirror targets alone did not.
span.quote: Since a repetition priming effect was found for small primes-identity targets (see results above) and no repetition priming effect was found for the identity prime-mirror reflected target condition (see statistics above), the lack of repetition effect for the small prime-mirror flipped target condition is primarily driven by the mirror reflection of the target.

span.label: Prime d' values near 1.7-1.8 versus target d' of 4.45-4.75 confirm that the masking kept primes below identification threshold at both prime sizes.
span.quote: The average d’ for food items appearing in the target position was 4.45 (significantly different from the prime items (t(23) = −9.436, p = 0.000) when preceded by a normal size non-food filler prime and 4.75 when preceded by a small non-food filler prime (significantly different from the prime items (t(23) = −10.275, p = 0.000).

span.label: identity condition
span.quote: The first condition constituted the identity condition , where the prime and the target were the exact same object.

span.label: size condition
span.quote: The second repetition condition was composed of a small prime (half the size of the target) that was the same object as the target item ( size condition ).

span.label: mirror condition
span.quote: The third repeated condition was composed of a prime and target pair where the target was a mirror flipped image of the prime ( mirror condition ).

span.label: size-mirror condition
span.quote: And finally, the fourth repetition condition consisted of a small prime followed by a target that was a normal size mirror flip of the prime ( size-mirror condition ).

span.label: repetition priming
span.quote: The typical behavioral effect observed in priming tasks is facilitation in reaction time or accuracy to target objects or words preceded by the same (so-called repetition priming) or a related prime in comparison to targets items preceded by unrelated or unrepeated primes.

span.label: N190/P190 component
span.quote: The N190/P190 component is thought to reflect early perceptual processing of objects ( Eddy et al., 2006 ).

span.label: N400 component
span.quote: The N400 is thought to reflect a general semantic mediated process or a process that activates a higher level representation of the object or word (e.g., Brown & Hagoort, 1993 ; Holcomb, 1993 ).

span.label: adaptation (fMRI repetition suppression)
span.quote: From the fMRI literature we know that adaptation or reduction in neural activity occurs when items are repeated, thought to indicate an overlap in the representation of the object.

span.label: prime size (normal vs half-size)
span.quote: We will test these hypotheses by examining differences in masked repetition priming effects for three manipulations: prime size, mirror reflection of target, and prime size-mirror reflection of target.

span.label: mirror reflection of the target
span.quote: In a second comparison, an ANOVA holding the size of the prime constant (as small) and manipulating whether or not the target was mirror reflected was examined.

span.label: repetition (repeated vs unrepeated prime-target pairs)
span.quote: Another four sets of 40 pairs of different, unrelated pictures of objects in the prime and target positions constituted the four unrepeated conditions where each of the manipulations mentioned above was present (identity, size, mirror, size-mirror - see Figure 1B ).

span.label: ERP mean amplitude in the N190/P190, N300 and N400 windows
span.term: ERP mean amplitude in the N190/P190, N300 and N400 windows
span.quote: Mean amplitude measurements were made in three time windows (early N190/P190 region 100–250 ms; N300 region 250–350 ms, and N400 region 350–500 ms).

span.label: electrode site (anterior-posterior column)
span.quote: The only electrode columns where repetition effects were more dependent on the size of the prime were the midline column and the peripheral column as indicated by a Repetition × Size × Electrode Site interaction (midline: F(4,92) = 5.289, p = 0.008, η p 2 = 0.187; peripheral: F(4,92) = 9.151, p = 0.003, η p 2 = .0285).

span.label: prime-target stimulus onset asynchrony and inter-trial interval
span.term: prime-target stimulus onset asynchrony and inter-trial interval
span.quote: The stimulus onset-asynchrony (SOA) for the prime and target was 110 ms, whereas the inter-trial interval was 3 seconds.

span.label: item assignment across conditions (counterbalanced lists)
span.quote: Twelve counterbalanced lists resulted in each repeated and unrepeated object being presented an equal number of times across participants, but each object being presented in only one trial for each participant.

span.label: number of artifact-free trials averaged per condition
span.term: number of artifact-free trials averaged per condition
span.quote: Approximately 34 items per condition were averaged (mean = 33.48, SD = 3.72) and the number of trials averaged per condition did not differ significantly (F(1,7) = 0.552, p = 0.771).

span.label: n = 24 — participants, undergraduates with a mean age of 19.6 years
span.quote: Twenty-four volunteers (13 female, M = 19.6 years old, SD = 1.2 years), undergraduate students at Tufts University, were paid $20 to participate in this experiment.

span.label: 620 — colour photographs of common objects used as stimuli, each 256 x 256 pixels
span.quote: Color photographs of 620 common objects (from Hemera Photo Objects), taken from conventional views, were displayed on a white background (each 256 × 256 pixels) on a 19-in. display (visual angle 2°) time-locked to the vertical refresh signal of the video card (100 Hz resolution).

span.label: 390 — trials viewed per subject, each a unique prime-target pair
span.quote: Each subject viewed 390 pseudorandomly arranged trials composed of a unique prime–target object pairs.

span.label: 110 ms — prime-target stimulus onset asynchrony held constant across conditions
span.quote: The stimulus onset-asynchrony (SOA) for the prime and target was 110 ms, whereas the inter-trial interval was 3 seconds.

span.label: 1.81 — d' for detecting a normal-size food prime (1.71 for a small food prime), indicating primes were not identifiable
span.quote: When a food prime was a normal size the d’ was 1.81 and when it was a small food prime the d’ was 1.71, suggesting that participants were NOT able to identify food objects in the prime position regardless of prime size (t(23) = 1.119, p = 0.275).

span.label: 4.45 — d' for food items in the target position after a normal-size filler prime (4.75 after a small prime)
span.quote: The average d’ for food items appearing in the target position was 4.45 (significantly different from the prime items (t(23) = −9.436, p = 0.000) when preceded by a normal size non-food filler prime and 4.75 when preceded by a small non-food filler prime (significantly different from the prime items (t(23) = −10.275, p = 0.000).

span.label: approximately 15% — trials discarded for blinks, eye movements or muscle artifact before averaging
span.quote: Trials with blinks, eye movements, and muscle artifact were rejected prior to averaging (approximately 15% of trials).

span.label: F(1,23) = 11.295, p = 0.003, η p 2 = 0.329 — midline main effect of repetition for the identity condition in the N400 window
span.quote: This effect was reflected by significant main effects of Repetition at all electrode columns (midline: F(1,23) = 11.295, p = 0.003, η p 2 = 0.329; medial: F(1,23) = 12.474, p = 0.002, η p 2 = 0.352; lateral: F(1,23) =13.688, p = 0.001, η p 2 = 0.373) and a significant interaction of Repetition with Electrode Site at the midline column (F(4,92) = 3.212, p = 0.041, η p 2 = 0.123).

span.label: F<3, p > 0.065 — non-significant repetition effect in the early window for the small-prime/mirror-target condition
span.quote: While significant repetition effects are observed for the small prime-identity target condition (see results above), when investigating repetition effects for the small prime – mirror reversal condition alone, no repetition effects are observed (F<3, p > 0.065) within this early time window (see Figure 6 and 7D ).

p.note: The full text of this article is not redistributable, so it is not included here. Every tag above carries the exact sentence it was made from, quoted under fair quotation. The article itself is at https://doi.org/10.1016/j.bandc.2009.05.006.
